title: Anticoagulants & Blood Collection Tubes

references.label: CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

summary: Blood collection tubes are color-coded by their additive (anticoagulant, clot activator, or gel separator), and the choice of tube determines which tests can validly be run on that draw.
explanation: Common additive families include: EDTA (chelates calcium; preserves cell morphology, standard for CBC/hematology), sodium citrate (chelates calcium in a fixed 9:1 blood-to-citrate ratio; used for coagulation testing such as PT/aPTT, where the ratio itself matters for result accuracy), heparin (activates antithrombin; used for some chemistry/stat panels and does not interfere with many electrolyte assays), sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate (inhibits glycolysis; used for glucose specimens where cells would otherwise continue consuming glucose in vitro), and plain or gel-separator clot-activator tubes (produce serum after clotting and centrifugation). Exact color-coding conventions are standardized within a manufacturer/system (e.g. lavender for EDTA, light blue for sodium citrate are widely used conventions) but a laboratory's own procedure manual is the authoritative source, since conventions can differ by manufacturer or region.

comparison.right: Used for: CBC, blood smear, differential

comparison.left: Chelates calcium at a fixed 9:1 ratio
comparison.right: Used for: PT/INR, aPTT — under-filling this tube invalidates the result

comparison.left: No anticoagulant; blood clots, then is centrifuged
comparison.right: Used for: most chemistry, serology when serum is required

commonMisconceptions: Assuming any anticoagulant tube can substitute for another because 'it's all just blood in a tube' — using the wrong additive can chelate an analyte being measured, inhibit an enzyme, or change cell morphology.
